summary: Star Commander is a browser game where students run a four-person Moon base on the rim of Shackleton crater, at the lunar south pole, for 30 days. Each day, players assign astronauts to jobs and balance power, life support, food and radiation shielding, which all compete for the same limited energy, cargo and time. It addresses the challenge of building a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer by making real engineering trade-offs tangible. Hazards such as a four-day shadow and a solar storm appear on a timeline, so every outcome comes from the player’s own plan, not luck. Each storm is a real flare from NASA’s DONKI space weather database, and its day-by-day shape follows radiation measured near the Moon by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. A Flight Director Debrief then explains what happened and why, turning every failure into a lesson. This matters because students usually read about space missions but never practise the decisions behind them. Star Commander offers three levels for ages 8 and up, runs in any browser with no login, and includes accessibility settings.
details:
Star Commander is a turn-based browser game. Students command four astronauts (a doctor, a botanist, a pilot and a geologist) at Shackleton crater on the lunar south pole for 30 days, called sols. Before launch, they choose two science objectives, load a cargo lander within a mass limit, and review the mission’s space weather. Each sol, they assign every astronaut a job, set life support to Full, Eco or Off, and decide whether to run the greenhouse lights.

How it Works:

A simulation then updates power, oxygen, water, food, shielding, crew health, stress and radiation dose. There are no random event cards. A timeline shows the hazards from day one: a four-day shadow when solar panels produce nothing, dust build-up, and a solar particle storm. Crew members also ask for decisions based on their own state, for example when the air is poor or their radiation dose is high. At the end, a Flight Director Debrief explains the key moments in two sentences each.

Benefits and impact:

The main benefit is learning by doing. Students usually read that the Sun can disappear for days or that solar storms are dangerous, but they never have to decide what to switch off. The intended impact is twofold:

  1. Practical learning: Students practise real mission trade-offs among power, life support, food and radiation protection. Three levels let the same game suit ages 8 to 13 and up, from simple status words to the equations behind each gauge.
  2. Interest in space careers: Named astronauts with different strengths, and a debrief that turns every failure into a lesson, make engineering feel personal and approachable.

It runs in any browser, on a phone or a school computer, with no login. It also offers an easy-read font, a colour-blind palette and a reduce-motion setting. We have not yet tested it in a classroom. That is our main next step.

Technology stack:

  • Languages and frameworks: JavaScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand for state. The simulation is a separate JavaScript module with no interface code.
  • Visuals: The Moon base, astronauts and charts are drawn as SVG in code.
  • Hosting: Deployed on Vercel, installable as an offline-capable web app, with progress saved in the browser.
  • Testing: A script plays five strategies automatically, so we could check the game’s balance without playing every run by hand.

Creativity and innovation:

Most space games for kids use random events. Star Commander shows its hazards in advance, the way real missions are planned, so students learn to plan rather than react to luck. Each astronaut has a name, a story and a specialty, and the crew’s own health, stress and radiation dose trigger their requests for decisions. The base itself is a live cutaway scene: a mound of Moon soil grows as shielding increases, and the whole base goes dark during the shadow. The innovation is turning NASA space weather records and radiation measurements into a game that a child can understand, without losing the real numbers.
